source_refs.note: Book p. 60-61: 2.12.1 Using dy to Approximate Δy, Fig. 2.7 and the box Using Differentials to Approximate

blocks.text: When a function \(y = f(x)\) is differentiable at a point \(P(x, y)\), we can use the differential \(dy\) to estimate the actual change \(\Delta y\) in \(y\), for small change \(\Delta x\) in \(x\).
The actual change \(\Delta y\) in \(y\) is given by:

blocks.text_alt: delta y equals f of (x plus delta x) minus f of x, equation (1)

blocks.text:
But calculating \(\Delta y\) exactly often requires complicated formulas. Instead, we use the differential \(dy\), defined as:
\[dy = f'(x)\,dx\]
If we take \(dx = \Delta x\), then:

blocks.text_alt: d y equals f prime of x times delta x, equation (2)

blocks.text: Let \(Q(x + \Delta x, f(x + \Delta x))\) be a neighboring point of \(P(x, y)\) on \(y = f(x)\).

items: The slope of the tangent line at \(P\) is \(f'(x)\)
The slope of the secant line connecting \(P\) and \(Q\) is \(\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}\)

blocks.text: As \(\Delta x \to 0\), the point \(Q\) approaches \(P\), and secant line \(PQ\) approaches the tangent line at \(P\). (See Fig. 2.7)

blocks.alt: Three graphs of the same rising curve. In each, P is a fixed point on the curve and Q another point on it, Delta x to the right. A green secant line joins P and Q and an orange tangent line touches the curve at P. From left to right Delta x gets smaller, Q moves towards P, and the secant line turns until it almost lies on the tangent line.
blocks.caption: Figure 2.7: as Δx shrinks, Q moves to P and the secant PQ approaches the tangent at P (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.text:
Therefore, for small \(\Delta x\):
slope of tangent line at \(P\) \(\approx\) slope of secant line \(PQ\)
\[\Rightarrow f'(x) \approx \dfrac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}\]
Substitute \(f'(x) \approx \frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}\) into equation (2):
\[dy \approx \dfrac{\Delta y}{\Delta x} \times \Delta x\]
\[dy \approx \Delta y \quad (\text{for } \Delta x \text{ is small})\]
Thus, for small change \(\Delta x\), the actual change \(\Delta y\) is approximately equal to the differential \(dy\), that is:

blocks.text_alt: delta y is approximately equal to d y, which equals f prime of x times d x

blocks.text:
Since \(\Delta y = f(x + \Delta x) - f(x)\) and for small change \(\Delta x\): \(dx = \Delta x\) and \(\Delta y \approx dy\).
\(\Rightarrow dy \approx f(x + \Delta x) - f(x)\)
and hence: \(f(x + \Delta x) \approx f(x) + dy\)
blocks.title: Using Differentials to Approximate:

blocks.text:
Two different changes, do not mix them up:
\(\Delta y\) = the real rise of the curve from \(x\) to \(x + \Delta x\) (exact, but may be hard to calculate).
\(dy\) = the rise of the tangent line over the same step (easy: slope times step).
For a small step the curve and the tangent hardly separate, so \(\Delta y \approx dy\).
blocks.title: Teaching note

blocks.text:
The last line of the box, \(f(x + \Delta x) \approx f(x) + dy = f(x) + f'(x)\,\Delta x\), is the same idea as linearization in 2.11.1: put \(a = x\) and \(x + \Delta x\) in place of \(x\) in \(L(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x - a)\).
It is the working formula for questions like "use differentials to approximate \(\sqrt{24}\)": known value \(f(x)\) plus the small correction \(dy\).
blocks.title: Teaching note

blocks.text:
1. Actual change: \(\Delta y = f(x + \Delta x) - f(x)\).
2. Differential: \(dy = f'(x)\,dx\), with \(dx = \Delta x\).
3. As \(\Delta x \to 0\) the secant \(PQ\) approaches the tangent at \(P\), so \(\Delta y \approx dy\) for small \(\Delta x\).
4. Approximation formula: \(f(x + \Delta x) \approx f(x) + f'(x)\,\Delta x\).
blocks.title: Key points

blocks.text:
1. Writing \(\Delta y = dy\) as exact; it is only \(\approx\).
2. Using the rule for a large \(\Delta x\): the secant is then far from the tangent and the estimate is poor.
3. Taking \(dx\) with the wrong sign: if \(x\) decreases, \(\Delta x\) is negative.
blocks.title: Common mistake
